body.hook: In Mandarin, the syllable "ma" can mean "mother," "hemp," "horse" or "scold," depending only on the tone of your voice. Say it the wrong way and "my mother" could become "my horse"! Tones are the key to being understood in Mandarin.

vocabulary.definition: The system that writes Chinese sounds with the Latin alphabet.
Tone: the pitch pattern of a syllable.
Neutral tone: light and short, with no tone mark (ma).

study.title: The Tone Ladder
study.question: How do tones change meaning in Mandarin?
study.passage:
The four tones on "ma":
• mā 妈 = mother (1st tone: high and flat, like singing a long note)
• má 麻 = hemp (2nd tone: rising, like asking "What?")
• mǎ 马 = horse (3rd tone: dips low then rises, like "Hmm?" when unsure)
• mà 骂 = scold (4th tone: sharp drop, like a firm "No!")
• ma 吗 = question word (neutral tone: light and short)
Hand signals: draw each tone in the air with your hand as you say it.
Sentence: 妈妈骂马吗？Māma mà mǎ ma? = Is Mom scolding the horse?
Tone change (sandhi): when two third tones come together, the first one changes to a second tone. 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but said "ní hǎo."
Activity 1, Tone ladder (10 minutes): The teacher says a syllable; students show 1, 2, 3 or 4 fingers.
Activity 2, Tone pairs (10 minutes): With a partner, say and identify: bā (eight) / bà (dad); shī / shí (shí = ten); mǎi (buy) / mài (sell).
Activity 3, Greet with tones: 你好！nǐ hǎo (hello), 谢谢 xièxie (thank you), 再见 zàijiàn (goodbye).
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

body.objective: Students will be able to read pinyin syllables.
successCriteria: I can identify initials and finals in pinyin syllables

body.hook: Every Mandarin syllable has three parts: a beginning sound (initial), an ending sound (final) and a tone. Pinyin, the official romanization system, lets you read any syllable before you know a single character.

vocabulary.definition: sounds like "j" in "jump" with the tongue curled back

study.title: Reading Pinyin
study.question: How do I read pinyin syllables?
study.passage:
Pinyin guide (written for this lesson):
A syllable = initial + final + tone. Example: mā = m (initial) + a (final) + first tone. Some syllables have no initial: ài (love), ěr (ear).
Initials that surprise English speakers: q = "ch" (as in cheese): qī (seven). x = "sh" (as in she): xiè (thank). j = "j" (as in jeep): jiā (home). zh = "j" with tongue curled back: zhōng (middle). ch = "ch" with tongue curled back: chī (eat). sh = "sh" with tongue curled back: shí (ten). z = "ds" (as in kids): zài (at). c = "ts" (as in cats): cài (dish). r = between English r and the s in "measure": rén (person).
Finals: a (father), o (more), e (like "uh"), i (see), u (moon), ü (say "ee" with rounded lips): nǚ (female).
Special: after zh, ch, sh, r, z, c, s, the i sounds like a buzzing "rr" or "zz," not "ee": shí, sì.
Activities: 1. Split syllables into initial and final on mini-whiteboards. 2. Teacher says a syllable; students hold up q, x, j, zh, ch or sh cards. 3. Partners read a list of 20 syllables aloud and check each other.

body.objective: Students will be able to use tone marks.
successCriteria: I can write tone marks on the correct vowel

body.hook: Mā, má, mǎ, mà: four tones, four different words (mother, hemp, horse, scold). Writing tone marks correctly is how readers know which word you mean.

study.title: Tone Marks
study.question: Where do tone marks go, and how do tones change?
study.passage:
Tone mark rules (written for this lesson):
1. If there is an a or e, it takes the mark: hǎo, xiè, gěi.
2. In ou, the o takes the mark: dōu, gǒu (dog).
3. Otherwise, the mark goes on the last vowel: in iu and ui, mark the second vowel: liù (six), duì (correct).
4. The dot on i disappears under a mark: nǐ, qī.
Neutral tone: light and short, no mark: māma (mom), xièxie (thanks), bàba (dad).
Third-tone change: when two third tones come together, the first becomes second tone: nǐ hǎo is said ní hǎo (but written nǐ hǎo).
不 bù change: before a fourth tone, bù becomes bú: bú shì (is not).
Activities: 1. Add tone marks to 20 syllables using the rules (e.g. hao3 → hǎo, liu4 → liù, gui4 → guì). 2. Tone dictation: teacher says syllables; students write pinyin with marks. 3. Partners practise nǐ hǎo, hěn hǎo, bú shì with the changes.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; rules follow standard pinyin conventions.
